2	('5dab36d2-be42-4dac-b4c3-9a1758a48326'::uuid,2,'Evaluate','On Main Conclusion questions, listen for the conclusion early. It usually shows up in the first sentence or right after a pivot that pushes back on someone else''s view.
3	
4	Here the first sentence does both. "Contrary to recent speculations" tells us other people expect a hardware store, and the author is about to disagree. Then comes the author''s own claim: no hardware store will be opening in the plaza.
5	
6	Test it by asking, "Why should I believe that?" The next two sentences answer. Anyone opening a store there would already be publicizing it, and there has been no publicity. So nobody is opening a store there. Both sentences point back at the first one, which makes the first sentence the main conclusion and the other two its evidence.
7	
8	The speculation itself is not the author''s view. It is the position the author argues against.'),
9	('5dab36d2-be42-4dac-b4c3-9a1758a48326'::uuid,3,'Goal','Find the answer that restates the author''s claim with the opener stripped off: a hardware store will not be opening in the shopping plaza. 10	('c97829cb-ce32-4ed7-b348-87a1a99191f7'::uuid,3,'Evaluate','The conclusion here sits in the middle sentence, and the word "For" is what gives it away. "For" means "because": the last sentence is the reason for the sentence before it. Why should we believe that expanding your mind lets you inspire curiosity? Because it makes you impossible to fully comprehend, so you stay a mystery to others.
11	
12	So what is the first sentence doing? It is called "a given." Nothing argues for it, and it is not a reason for the middle sentence either. It explains why anyone would care about inspiring curiosity. That makes it background, not the conclusion.
13	
14	Now the hard part: the conclusion is a conditional, so direction matters. The author says expanding your mind is enough to inspire curiosity:
15	
16	Expands mind → Inspires others'' curiosity

20	('737e7000-49dd-46b2-b774-be961f17f175'::uuid,2,'Evaluate','On Main Conclusion questions, check the first sentence first. It is often the claim, with the reasons following it.
21	
22	The manager opens with an opinion: there is no good reason to suppose promoting creativity is a proper goal of employee training. Ask, "Why should I believe that?" The rest of the paragraph answers. Reason one: many jobs need little or no creativity, and in those jobs creativity is more likely to disrupt than to innovate. Reason two, flagged by "Furthermore": even if creativity were in demand, there is no evidence it can be taught.
23	
24	"Furthermore" stacks a second reason on the first. Both point back at the opening sentence, so that sentence is the main conclusion.
25

27	('737e7000-49dd-46b2-b774-be961f17f175'::uuid,3,'Goal','Look for an answer that matches the first sentence, including its caution: there is no good reason to suppose employee training programs should promote creativity. 28	('1da55640-b0da-40a2-bb51-02ea734fb642'::uuid,4,'Evaluate','On Main Conclusion questions, listen for the moment the author''s own voice arrives. Here the first two sentences belong to the many people the anthropologist is answering: chimpanzees should have something like language, because traits evolve gradually and something like human language must exist in the species humans evolved from.
29	
30	Then the pivot: "This general line of argument may be reasonable, but". The anthropologist grants the gradual-evolution reasoning and rejects only one step of it, the jump to chimpanzees. The claim after "but" is the author''s position.

32	Check it with "Why should I believe that?" The answer follows the word "because": humans did not evolve from chimpanzees. Chimps are relatives through a common ancestor, and language might have started after that ancestor died out. So even if something like language must exist in species humans evolved from, chimpanzees are not one of those species, and nothing follows about them.

43	
44	A useful check on Main Conclusion: when a pivot word like "However" is followed later by a support word like "for," the conclusion often sits between them.'),
45	('722eee11-4785-4f6f-a706-d61d1b78535b'::uuid,'32993111d898b7bb283fe9fbddbd811c','E widens the claim. B keeps both the comparison and "may."
48	
49	When a conclusion uses a word like "that" to point back, work out what it refers to before you match. The right answer will usually spell it out, as B does.'),

52	('bccd5dc9-a22c-4ba7-8cbc-1e6d250e4ed9'::uuid,'3112006946becc6bbb4276d3522b003d','E links home banking to banks eliminating branches and staff. 53	('dadf5035-217f-4572-a398-46eefb908320'::uuid,'e210cd25beb7c5328063fc0d15c183b4','A takes the evidence about social movements and inflates it. On Main Conclusion, the right answer can be a more general restatement of the claim, as long as it says nothing the author didn''t.'),
59	('11e05fdf-74f6-4679-9730-914509d5450f'::uuid,'0ab71b839ed6fdefad665fbf053744cf','Emotional impact never comes up. Tool call: mcp__d2692868-3949-490b-864d-de2c41e9f9b7__query_database
{"project_id": "53b9a6f2-aba7-4ae4-8dd1-fa5b8aab4d76", "sql": "insert into lr_explanation_steps (explanation_id,position,label,body) select v.e,v.p,v.l,v.b from (values\n('5dab36d2-be42-4dac-b4c3-9a1758a48326'::uuid,2,'Evaluate','On Main Conclusion questions, listen for the conclusion early. It usually shows up in the first sentence or right after a pivot that pushes back on someone else''s view.\n\nHere the first sentence does both. \"Contrary to recent speculations\" tells us other people expect a hardware store, and the author is about to disagree. Then comes the author''s own claim: no hardware store will be opening in the plaza.\n\nTest it by asking, \"Why should I believe that?\" The next two sentences answer. Anyone opening a store there would already be publicizing it, and there has been no publicity. So nobody is opening a store there. Both sentences point back at the first one, which makes the first sentence the main conclusion and the other two its evidence.\n\nThe speculation itself is not the author''s view. It is the position the author argues against.'),\n('5dab36d2-be42-4dac-b4c3-9a1758a48326'::uuid,3,'Goal','Find the answer that restates the author''s claim with the opener stripped off: a hardware store will not be opening in the shopping plaza. Expect trap answers that restate the speculation, the conditional premise, or the no-publicity premise.'),\n('c97829cb-ce32-4ed7-b348-87a1a99191f7'::uuid,3,'Evaluate','The conclusion here sits in the middle sentence, and the word \"For\" is what gives it away. \"For\" means \"because\": the last sentence is the reason for the sentence before it. Why should we believe that expanding your mind lets you inspire curiosity? Because it makes you impossible to fully comprehend, so you stay a mystery to others.\n\nSo what is the first sentence doing? It is called \"a given.\" Nothing argues for it, and it is not a reason for the middle sentence either. It explains why anyone would care about inspiring curiosity. That makes it background, not the conclusion.\n\nNow the hard part: the conclusion is a conditional, so direction matters. The author says expanding your mind is enough to inspire curiosity:\n\nExpands mind → Inspires others'' curiosity\n\nThe author does not say it is the only way. An answer that flips this into a requirement, or that changes whose curiosity we are talking about, is a different claim.'),\n('c97829cb-ce32-4ed7-b348-87a1a99191f7'::uuid,4,'Goal','Look for an answer that says: if you constantly broaden your abilities and extend your intellectual reach, you will be able to inspire the perpetual curiosity of others. Check the direction (broadening is the trigger, curiosity is the result) and check that the curiosity belongs to other people.'),\n('737e7000-49dd-46b2-b774-be961f17f175'::uuid,2,'Evaluate','On Main Conclusion questions, check the first sentence first. It is often the claim, with the reasons following it.\n\nThe manager opens with an opinion: there is no good reason to suppose promoting creativity is a proper goal of employee training. Ask, \"Why should I believe that?\" The rest of the paragraph answers. Reason one: many jobs need little or no creativity, and in those jobs creativity is more likely to disrupt than to innovate. Reason two, flagged by \"Furthermore\": even if creativity were in demand, there is no evidence it can be taught.\n\n\"Furthermore\" stacks a second reason on the first. Both point back at the opening sentence, so that sentence is the main conclusion.\n\nNotice how careful the conclusion is. The manager does not say training should never promote creativity. Here the first two sentences belong to the many people the anthropologist is answering: chimpanzees should have something like language, because traits evolve gradually and something like human language must exist in the species humans evolved from.\n\nThen the pivot: \"This general line of argument may be reasonable, but\". The anthropologist grants the gradual-evolution reasoning and rejects only one step of it, the jump to chimpanzees. The claim after \"but\" is the author''s position.\n\nCheck it with \"Why should I believe that?\" The answer follows the word \"because\": humans did not evolve from chimpanzees. Chimps are relatives through a common ancestor, and language might have started after that ancestor died out. So even if something like language must exist in species humans evolved from, chimpanzees are not one of those species, and nothing follows about them.\n\nNotice how limited the conclusion is. The author does not say chimpanzees lack language. 2	('49a6cf2d-3ad4-48a5-805a-d29fd8627b5f'::uuid,'1689a34952a2fd21858ef29706c6c9b0','The blank comes after "since", so it is the conclusion, and everything before it is the evidence. Let''s line up what happens to the workers.
3	
4	Mass production lowered prices by using fewer workers, many of whom needed little training. Lower prices let workers buy goods they could not afford before. That''s a gain.
5	
6	Then the pivot: "But since" jobs needing little training are more vulnerable to elimination. That''s a cost, and it lands on exactly the kind of job mass production relies on.
7	
8	So one cause, mass production, does two things to the same people. It raises what they can buy, and it makes their jobs less secure. The "But" tells us the conclusion should bring in the downside without erasing the upside.','Evaluate','Evaluate'),
9	('61d0699b-ae2f-4f00-8933-8c2be2ded79f'::uuid,'8b9a0c23e6c20db17fc413cb809448b1','Predict a modest answer that ties the two together: the same thing that boosted workers'' buying power also left their jobs more exposed. 10	('90bd8980-9a76-4618-9087-855534bd9189'::uuid,'fef9249ddaf26ac57bea76be29cbb9f4','Start with the structure. "Although" opens a concession: a single application gives short-term gains. "We should conclude that" marks the blank as the conclusion, and the sentence just before it, that long-term use gradually depresses yield, is the evidence driving it.
11	
12	Now read that evidence closely. Yields go up at first, then slide down "from this initially elevated level". It doesn''t say yields fall below where they started. 14	('415fba4f-484e-4b5c-9ee4-d1a76847e01f'::uuid,'f30b129479cf8cadaf3adead653c531d','  - *Contrast:* mu mesons (MMs) generated by cosmic rays just outside Earth''s atmosphere travel at speeds approaching the speed of light, **whereas** MMs generated in the lab are nearly at rest.
15	  - *Comparison:* a lab MM typically decays in much less time than it takes an MM to travel from just outside the atmosphere to our detector on Earth.
16	  - *Conditional:* if fast MMs typically decay as fast as lab MMs, then we should detect only about one one-hundredth of the number **we actually do detect.**','Given','Given'),
17	('999a1eb1-7e4b-4d8e-84b2-85a83ef89eef'::uuid,'8bdcf002c72ee1e62ecde6af54a3c5d5','Let''s call mu mesons MMs. The fast ones are made just outside the atmosphere and travel to Earth at nearly the speed of light. The lab ones are nearly at rest, and they typically decay in much less time than the trip from the upper atmosphere to our detector takes.
18	
19	The fourth sentence does the real work. It''s a conditional:
20	
21	fast MMs decay as fast as lab MMs → we detect about 1/100 of the number we actually detect
22	
23	Read the right side carefully. We can''t detect one one-hundredth of the number we actually detect. We detect the number we actually detect. So the right side is false, and when the right side of a conditional is false, the left side has to be false too. That''s the contrapositive:
24	
25	NOT detect 1/100 of the actual number → fast MMs do NOT decay as fast as lab MMs
26	
27	So the fast MMs don''t decay as fast as the lab ones. The blank is about "mu mesons moving at speeds near the speed of light", which are the fast ones. The sentence should finish by saying they decay more slowly than the MMs at rest.','Evaluate','Evaluate'),
28	('3e43ec14-0387-4b38-bfd3-38d94d029a21'::uuid,'5747a9737e0171967f8822b826b546fe','Look past the physics words and the prediction is short: MMs moving near the speed of light decay more slowly than MMs at rest in the lab. An answer about travel time, detection equipment, how many MMs there are, or where they come from leaves the conditional untouched.','Goal','Goal'),
29	('d1e3b047-7252-426f-b3f0-72cfadb06b9f'::uuid,'d19c85c61a09c2cba1e294926d00571d','Three facts about superstring theory. It purports to explain the nature and existence of gravity, which more established theories don''t even try to do. Testing it would take a particle accelerator 100 trillion kilometers long. And it has had no success explaining why gravity is as strong as it is, neither stronger nor weaker.
30	
31	The second and third facts are both called a "problem". That word carries a judgment, so ask why. Why would failing to explain gravity''s strength count against this theory? Because the theory claims to explain gravity. A theory that sets out to explain a force and can''t say why the force has the strength it has is falling short of its own job.
32	
33	Notice what the stimulus does not give us: anything about what the established theories have achieved, whether superstring theory is true, or how hard the theorists have tried.','Evaluate','Evaluate'),
34	('ba9171cd-c81d-4217-9c6b-7ecfc7d213c2'::uuid,'5b1bc959c4c2b07c36db20d64f2a6d2f','There''s no conditional chain to link, so we want the answer that rests on what the stimulus says or clearly implies. 35	('1e8e2fc0-11a1-4b69-8992-84747db42253'::uuid,'904dc4f9127918646128284f582be7b8','Cerrato reports two claims from economists. First, part-time workers are much more likely to be dissatisfied with their jobs than full-time workers. Second, part-time workers threaten to take jobs from full-time employees. Then the pivot, "But": job efficiency goes with job satisfaction, so companies are unlikely to replace satisfied employees with dissatisfied ones.
36	
37	Put the pieces together. If part-timers are the dissatisfied ones, and companies won''t swap satisfied workers for dissatisfied ones, then companies won''t swap full-timers for those part-timers. That undercuts the second claim. Cerrato is turning the economists'' first claim against their second: the two don''t fit together.
38	
39	Notice that Cerrato never says the first claim is true, only that economists argue it. So the safest completion is tied to it: to the extent part-timers are dissatisfied, they aren''t a threat to full-time jobs. Predict an answer saying dissatisfied part-time workers are unlikely to take full-timers'' jobs.','Evaluate / Goal','Evaluate / Goal'),
40	('b6179904-d450-4140-a885-cb87c7173964'::uuid,'617bae7c4f722556d6a5823aae04c92d','Three statements, and the last one pivots.
41	
42	1. Comparison: dark honey tends to have a higher antioxidant content than light-colored honey.
43	
44	2. Rule: the most healthful strains of honey are all unusually high in antioxidants.
45	most healthful strain → unusually high in antioxidants
46	
47	3. Pivot ("However"): certain strains from bees harvesting primarily sage nectar are among the most healthful strains, even though they are among the lightest-colored.','Information','Information'),
48	('147da0b5-3a6b-44e8-8a93-c202fd85f11c'::uuid,'ac39d50d8dc170f9e06f38ff0aabc543','The first statement tempts us to link color and health: dark honey has more antioxidants, the healthiest honey has lots of antioxidants, so maybe the healthiest honey is dark. The "However" stops that. Some of the most healthful strains are among the lightest.
49	
50	Now look for a fact that triggers a rule. Statement 3 tells us certain sage-nectar strains are among the most healthful. Statement 2 says every one of the most healthful strains is unusually high in antioxidants. Put them together:
51	
52	certain sage-nectar strains → most healthful → unusually high in antioxidants
53	
54	So those sage-nectar strains are unusually high in antioxidants, even though they are light-colored. That''s provable. Notice also what statement 1 doesn''t do: "tends to" is only a trend, so a light honey with lots of antioxidants doesn''t contradict it.','Evaluate','Evaluate'),
55	('f1aab2c1-3405-4b63-8310-541591d03bb9'::uuid,'62df54a15a4f3e946a427b582419ae67','Look for the answer that combines statements 2 and 3: some sage-nectar honey is unusually high in antioxidants. 56	('e86242f3-17e6-401e-8a9e-1e92b3ddd0ee'::uuid,'4df57f4fc3a5054c9532dbfefdfe5e17','Predict that the strategy backfires: by giving up traditions that are each essential to the culture''s identity, the culture loses what makes it that culture. 57	('1022806f-ccbe-4ddc-bce5-e4e2b7094421'::uuid,'afa26c5d44c275efaf4cdf0c4a2574b4','In the past, infants who weren''t breast-fed were fed cow''s milk.
58	Doctors then advised boiling that milk to sterilize it and prevent gastrointestinal infections potentially fatal to infants.
59	Once the advice was widely followed, scurvy (caused by vitamin C deficiency) rose alarmingly among infants.
60	Breast-fed infants did not get scurvy.','Information','Information'),
61	('70b5db2e-ad06-426b-865b-d18a2658ac18'::uuid,'f6c023b7b4e2329a769d251b50041d9b','Start with the timing. Before the advice, infants who weren''t breast-fed drank cow''s milk. Once boiling became widespread, scurvy rose sharply. Scurvy comes from a lack of vitamin C. Breast-fed infants, who never got the boiled milk, didn''t get scurvy.
62	
63	So one difference (boiled cow''s milk versus mother''s milk) lines up with another difference (scurvy versus no scurvy), and we''re told what causes scurvy. The simplest way to connect them: infants on boiled cow''s milk weren''t getting enough vitamin C, and breast-fed infants were. The rise came right after boiling caught on, which suggests the boiling cut the vitamin C, but we don''t need the mechanism. We only need the comparison.','Evaluate','Evaluate'),
64	('d704cfb4-caee-401d-b748-0ee675cad940'::uuid,'6e8fb0c0269c6f2a66120b8f4ebd3940','This is a reasonable inference, not a certainty, and that''s fine on Most Strongly Supported. Watch for answers that add a frequency, a state of knowledge, or a proportion the passage never mentions.','Goal','Goal')

19	('540c51d2-ba18-45b2-a306-fc3e72ea3496'::uuid,'3c23a1121f1166127caf1645c6a4a526','This is the trap that sounds careful, because "some" and "at least some success" are weak wording. 33	('bfd05df2-16ad-4a38-a16e-148fdbc232d7'::uuid,'3de58cd6bddfc1c390de2002ce091942','Chain it. The strategy gives up many traditions. Each tradition is essential to the culture''s identity. 35	('ea2d9fc3-f9ba-4f04-be79-6947532dfa28'::uuid,'50867c1ccd1ddaa466cf0be48c7d912e','This is the anthropologists'' claim, nearly word for word. 36	('9df27a6f-3c51-4329-af28-bc801041a41d'::uuid,'5d357191484a7247b797a59a7fb9ce02','The premise says "each" tradition is essential, old or new. 37	('f2093996-b3cf-4ee8-a342-b41e2cf75833'::uuid,'748cfeaf226fccead7ad28d88c3d26df','This matches the prediction. 3	
4	Instinctual behavior → no reasoning, far fewer nerve cells than flexible behavior
5	Capable of flexible behavior → large number of neurons
6	Insect brain → NOT a large enough number of neurons
7

9	('e3ecd26c-6ee4-45e6-b372-59815aabb17f'::uuid,'5f714ef466d67de47c932a3889d7bfdc','On Must Be True, conditionals and shared terms come first. Do any of these rules share a term?
10	
11	Yes. The second and third both talk about a large number of neurons. The second says flexible behavior requires it. The third says insect brains don''t have it. Take the contrapositive of the second (NOT large number of neurons → NOT capable of flexible behavior) and attach it to the third:
12	
13	Insect brain → NOT large number of neurons → NOT capable of flexible behavior
14	
15	And since anything that isn''t flexible is instinctual, insect behavior is instinctual.
16	
17	Notice what this chain can''t do. A large number of neurons is a requirement for flexible behavior, not a guarantee. So we know what lacking the neurons rules out. Having them proves nothing.','Evaluate','Evaluate'),
18	('62386109-6b6c-4f51-8d1b-13c3913491b4'::uuid,'546b92308a57140ae8082c4e204df2cb','Predict the end of the chain: insects can''t behave flexibly, so insect behavior is instinctual.
19	
20	Expect traps that read the neuron requirement backwards, treating a large brain as enough for flexible behavior, or treating a small brain as the only route to pure instinct.','Goal','Goal'),
21	('7285cc2f-730b-43ea-9b38-8bee4d9fa61f'::uuid,'7f3b9dd555146ac91a9170922358b9d6','Three rules about which authors make the book.
22	
23	1. At least one of Lind, Knight, and Jones is in. ("Lind, Knight, or Jones")
24	2. Not all three are in.
25	3. K → J
26	
27	Rule 3 is the one with a consequence. Pick Knight and Jones comes along. Now we have two of the three, and rule 2 says the third can''t join. So:
28	
29	K → J → ~L
30	
31	Lind is blocked whenever Knight is in. Take the contrapositive:
32	
33	L → ~K
34	
35	Notice what we can''t say. Knight doesn''t have to be in. Lind doesn''t have to be in. A book with Jones alone breaks no rule, and neither does a book with Lind alone. Rules like these limit combinations. They don''t force any single author into the book.','Evaluate','Evaluate'),
36	('3255122f-8444-46fe-ae1e-0511d98cc1fd'::uuid,'2af9df59099d977ac16280798b153c0e','Only people who are **willing to compromise** should undergo **mediation** to resolve their conflicts.

40	Actual **litigation** should be pursued only when one is **sure** that one''s position is **correct**.
41	
42	L → SC
43	
44	People whose **conflicts are based on ideology** are **unwilling to compromise**.
45	
46	I → ~WC','Explanation','Statements'),
47	('01749785-9dae-492e-b4b5-e0d8f392ec68'::uuid,'cc1b1ded35b29a385f13da306c26a4cc','Although some nutritional facts about soft drinks are listed on their labels, exact caffeine content is not.

52	
53	If it became easier for people to limit, but not eliminate, their caffeine intake, many people would do so, which would improve their health.
54	Easier to limit → Many people limit → Their health improves','Given','Given'),
55	('f5f44b74-357b-411f-83c9-46f59f9143e8'::uuid,'a020e58193951bcadf27d63cf29e5b65','Claim 1: For several decades, the number of transistors on new microchips has doubled about every 18 months, "and hence" so has computing speed. Each doubling in transistors brought a doubling in speed.

2	('3937fc73-7987-4439-80cc-6b64375df558'::uuid,1,'Goal','Since nothing forces any one author in or out, expect a conditional answer: K → ~L or its contrapositive, L → ~K.
3	
4	Any answer that makes a flat claim about one author, or about how many authors appear, can be tested the same way: build a legal book that breaks it. If you can, it doesn''t have to be true.'),
5	('1df1c56c-2734-48a2-9856-6a70bf7258cb'::uuid,1,'Evaluate','Three conditionals. Is there a term they share?
6	
7	Willingness to compromise shows up twice. Mediation requires it (first rule), and ideological conflicts lack it (third rule). That overlap is the hinge. Flip the first rule with its contrapositive and attach it to the third:
8	
9	I → ~WC
10	~WC → ~M
11	
12	So: I → ~WC → ~M.
13	
14	What about litigation? L → SC shares no term with the other two. Being sure of your position never connects to compromise or ideology, so that rule is a dead end. Any answer that bridges it to the others is inventing a link.'),
15	('1df1c56c-2734-48a2-9856-6a70bf7258cb'::uuid,2,'Goal','Predict I → ~M: people in ideological conflicts should not undergo mediation.
16	
17	Then watch for two traps: answers that start from a negated trigger or a necessary condition (those trigger nothing), and answers that try to connect the litigation rule to anything else.'),
18	('73c0e56c-6943-42cd-ac7c-f2720d27b25d'::uuid,1,'Evaluate','Look for the shared term. "Easier to limit, but not eliminate" is the result of the second sentence and the trigger of the third. That lets us chain them:
19	
20	Listed → Easier to limit → Many people limit → Their health improves
21	
22	Now the first sentence. It''s a fact, and it negates the start of the chain: caffeine content is not listed. A negated trigger tells us nothing, so the chain only describes what would happen if the content were listed. Any answer about what happens because it isn''t listed is going past the statements.'),
23	('73c0e56c-6943-42cd-ac7c-f2720d27b25d'::uuid,2,'Goal','Predict the chain from start to finish, kept hypothetical: if exact caffeine content were listed, some people''s health would improve.
24	
25	Watch for answers that run the chain from "not listed," and answers that swap limiting for eliminating.'),
26	('fa9d395e-6f34-483b-8af6-e2d7a964a3f2'::uuid,1,'Evaluate','Three conditionals, and they overlap. More consumers is the result of the second and the trigger of the first. Higher profits is the result of the first and the trigger of the third ("not increase unless" puts lower congestion on the necessary side). Line them up:
27	
28	↓CL → ↑C → ↑P → ↓TC
29	
30	Read the chain like a one-way street. Anything on the left guarantees everything to its right. Nothing on the right guarantees anything to its left. Lower congestion is required for higher profits, but it doesn''t produce them.
31	
32	The contrapositive runs the other way with every term negated: if congestion doesn''t fall, profits won''t rise, the number of residents won''t increase, and the cost of living won''t decrease.'),
33	('fa9d395e-6f34-483b-8af6-e2d7a964a3f2'::uuid,2,'Goal','Every answer is a conditional, so the test is direction. A correct answer moves left to right along the chain, or right to left with both sides negated. Expect something like ↓CL → ↑P, ↑C → ↓TC, or ↓CL → ↓TC.
34	
35	Any answer that starts at ↓TC and claims something follows is backwards.'),
36	('fa360b2e-cdb0-4824-80b2-17740d6bbb08'::uuid,1,'Evaluate','What do the two claims share? Doubling in computing speed. Claim 1 ties each transistor doubling to a speed doubling. Claim 2 ties each speed doubling, in that window, to a cost doubling. Connect them through the shared term:
37	
38	Transistors double → speed doubles → (mid-1990s into next decade) cost doubles
39	
40	Now notice the limits. The cost fact covers only the mid-1990s into the next decade. Nothing tells us why costs doubled, what happened to the retail price of computers, what engineers were trying to do, or whether the pattern will continue.'),
41	('fa360b2e-cdb0-4824-80b2-17740d6bbb08'::uuid,2,'Goal','Predict the substitution, with its time window intact: from the mid-1990s into the next decade, each doubling in transistors came with a doubling in production cost.
42	
43	Expect wrong answers to stretch past what was reported: the only way to raise speed, retail prices, engineers'' motives, or the future.'),
44	('92c75e79-e4b4-40b3-a28b-6e2b1286aeb1'::uuid,1,'Evaluate','The only conditional is the last sentence. Addictive substances have to be hard to quit for most users. Contrapositive: if withdrawal does not cause most users extreme difficulty, the substance is not addictive.
45	
46	Now ask what the rejected test missed. A few users quitting tells us about some users. The requirement is about most users. Both can be true at once: a substance can be easy to quit for a handful and brutal for the majority. That''s exactly how the prime examples of addictive substances slip past the some-users test.
47	
48	Notice also what the rule can''t do. It gives a requirement for addictiveness. It never says what is enough to make something addictive.'),
49	('92c75e79-e4b4-40b3-a28b-6e2b1286aeb1'::uuid,2,'Goal','Expect an answer that applies the requirement in the right direction, probably playing some against most: a substance some users quit easily can still be addictive, but only if most users have a hard time.
50	
51	Be ready to reject answers that treat the requirement as sufficient, or that talk about one person instead of most users.'),
52	('6f0a8af5-c592-4ba7-b022-e821e909ea5d'::uuid,1,'Evaluate','Watch the modal words. Rule 1 says "are to be preserved": a requirement. Rule 2 says "may": permission, not a duty. Rule 3 also says "may." An answer that turns a "may" into a "should" goes beyond the manual.
53	
54	Then watch the triggers. Rule 2 needs only one thing: archaic material from an older work that occurs frequently. Whether it interferes doesn''t matter. Rule 3 covers obvious typos in modern works, not archaic spellings. And the manual is silent about some cases, like an archaic form that occurs infrequently but does interfere. Neither rule 1 nor rule 2 triggers there, so nothing follows.'),
55	('6f0a8af5-c592-4ba7-b022-e821e909ea5d'::uuid,2,'Goal','Look for an answer that triggers a rule cleanly and keeps its strength. The likeliest shape: archaic spelling or punctuation from an older work that occurs frequently may be modernized. Extra details are fine as long as the whole trigger is there.')
56	) v(e,p,l,b) where not exists (select 1 from lr_explanation_steps x where x.explanation_id=v.e and x.position=v.p) returning id;

1	update lr_explanation_choice_notes t set body=v.nb from (values
2	('db4dc1df-5fab-4cd9-b137-b0d1cb3ef2c2'::uuid,'aa23d2dc7138ef03f1debf9daafb5eb2','"Usually not instinctual" is a claim about how organisms with elaborate brains actually behave. The stimulus gives a requirement for flexible behavior, so it can only tell us who can''t behave flexibly. An organism with plenty of neurons could still run on instinct most of the time without breaking any statement.'),
3	('fde33acb-dc48-4914-ae5d-4ea0b6e14c71'::uuid,'c106d3c01b1f4e31bd497874f5fbad99','Run the chain from insects. No insect brain provides a sufficiently large number of neurons, and flexible behavior requires one, so no insect brain is capable of flexible behavior. The stimulus defines flexible as noninstinctual, so whatever insects do is instinctual.
4	
5	"Exclusively" sounds strong, but it''s earned: the requirement is missing for every insect, so there is no room for even a little flexible behavior. When a strong word shows up on Must Be True, check whether a universal rule (here, "no insect brain") backs it before crossing it off.'),
6	('06296952-c65d-422b-814b-1714860093e6'::uuid,'b87904bb0419e9d44d1b66bac8d90a15','Larger than an insect''s brain isn''t the same as large enough. The stimulus only says insect brains fall short. A brain could beat an insect''s and still lack the neurons. And even a brain with enough neurons isn''t guaranteed flexible behavior, because the neuron count is a requirement, not a guarantee.'),
7	('a804f0e2-9d72-492b-9f50-465b9ca0598b'::uuid,'a738854f62018292603520cd1eea31cf','This reverses the rule. Capable of flexible behavior → large number of neurons says the neurons are required. D reads it as large brain → equipped for flexible behavior, treating the requirement as enough. Driving legally requires a license, but holding a license doesn''t make someone a driver. D also swaps "large brain" for "large number of neurons," which the stimulus never equates.'),
8	('364af33b-7f64-43bb-86c8-340bfd18bdc1'::uuid,'42b75ffe4b1127a15f32646c53134d8a','E says purely instinctual → brain of insect size or smaller. We only know the other direction: insect → instinctual. An organism with a bigger brain that still falls short of the neuron count would also be limited to instinct, and nothing rules that out. "Only" makes a small brain a requirement for pure instinct, and the stimulus never sets that requirement.'),
9	('056ef2d1-49b7-4b02-9413-37c76abe8f04'::uuid,'7c6f201bc777c7e136e120aa94019118','This is the contrapositive we built. Suppose Lind is in and Knight is also in. Knight drags Jones in, and now the book has all three, which rule 2 forbids. So Lind in means Knight out.
10	
11	The move to repeat: when one rule forces an item to bring a second, check whether that pair runs into a limit (here, "not all three") that blocks a third. That blocked combination is often the inference.'),
12	('3da72e13-099e-4e71-8017-9ce07d568803'::uuid,'ed314d846335c68a1e203a5aa65560b7','Only one author? Build a legal book with two: Knight and Jones. Rule 1 is met, rule 2 is met because Lind is out, and Knight brought Jones as rule 3 demands. Two authors and no broken rule, so B doesn''t have to be true.'),
13	('bfd9faf1-42e7-437a-8694-114278eaf426'::uuid,'edb19383c949514b98bccb3bb00a4d85','Knight can be in. A book with Knight and Jones and no Lind satisfies every rule. The rules only say that Knight''s presence has consequences (Jones in, Lind out). They never exclude Knight.'),
14	('4aea2107-e33a-476a-8976-9d0a8ff528dd'::uuid,'8d964525edaaf41407e4b0b4da305de9','Lind doesn''t bring Jones. A book with Lind alone satisfies all three rules: at least one author, not all three, and rule 3 never triggers because Knight is absent. So L → J doesn''t have to hold. D borrows Jones from the Knight rule and attaches it to Lind.'),
15	('505588b9-5225-42bd-b00f-be2dd5519c9d'::uuid,'3d5bb50911c444dd8f1bbd807e61c5a8','Lind isn''t required. A book with Knight and Jones satisfies every rule without Lind, and so does a book with Jones alone. Rule 1 says at least one of the three is in, not which one.'),
16	('f911fdd7-afab-4167-af27-26f26553d414'::uuid,'8d5f2d0d11f068832e58f398208f3441','A starts from people who do not undergo mediation. That negates the trigger of the first rule, so it tells us nothing. And to reach "should be sure," A has to assume these people should litigate. Nothing says that someone who skips mediation should go to court. They could drop the conflict entirely.'),
17	('bff43783-8559-4be8-87d1-ed77f11a82ca'::uuid,'e4e5d49dbddc90119c06fa664552d1a6','Not based on ideology negates the trigger of the third rule, so we learn nothing about compromise. Even if we did, no rule ever says anyone should pursue litigation. The litigation rule only gives a requirement (being sure), never a recommendation.'),
18	('e4f4654f-7376-4704-8718-90428d405d04'::uuid,'c35a955777515e0e0e39b8f6d82b00c8','C connects ideology to being sure. The rules link ideology to compromise, and compromise to mediation. Being sure only appears in the litigation rule, which connects to nothing else. People in ideological conflicts could be completely sure of themselves without breaking any rule.'),
19	('080c7abc-5921-4fd1-b619-c4b96d25c39e'::uuid,'97bb71fb72d216b55b90b950fff30513','Being sure is the necessary side of the litigation rule, so it can''t trigger anything. D also ties sureness to mediation, but sureness never touches compromise. Someone sure of their position and willing to compromise could undergo mediation, and no rule says otherwise.'),
20	('a280a233-6f6c-4923-b295-fee7b5205c3e'::uuid,'62cef43d1edbb227819344e620bf9af9','Chain the third rule into the contrapositive of the first. I → ~WC, and ~WC → ~M. So I → ~M: people whose conflicts are based on ideology are not people who should undergo mediation. That''s E.
21	
22	The move: find the term two rules share (willingness to compromise), line the rules up so the shared term sits in the middle, flipping one with its contrapositive if needed, and read off the two ends.'),
23	('0f5087ba-df7c-499e-bf24-5b56650c1294'::uuid,'27b3dd5cdc7947223e8c1be8610ed9d3','This is the chain read end to end, in the same hypothetical mood as the stimulus. Listed → easier to limit → many people limit → their health improves. "Many people" guarantees "at least some people," so the weaker wording is safely proven.
24	
25	Notice A says "would" and "if exact caffeine content were listed." It doesn''t claim anyone''s health is improving now, which matters because the first sentence tells us the content isn''t listed. A good Must Be True answer keeps both the chain and its conditions.'),
26	('ceecc249-0dfe-43e7-81fa-a32d74805625'::uuid,'a1f19720da4ca4a30ae93ecbd2f5cc6a','B starts from the actual situation: content not listed. That negates the trigger of the second statement, and a negated trigger proves nothing. The stimulus says listing would make limiting easier. It never says people can''t limit at all without it. B turns "easier" into "possible."'),
27	('b88a2b33-fa8d-4d1e-b886-b2d24a79f699'::uuid,'90ad818fa815e8b4b94900f7517a8fce','C also starts from content not being listed (people have to guess), and then switches from limiting to eliminating. The stimulus is explicit that listing would help people limit, "but not eliminate," their intake. It says nothing about how hard eliminating is when people have to guess.'),
28	('46dd0aeb-c5da-48cd-aa91-fa90a4831a7d'::uuid,'5c1033db9fbd855320925645026f9dfe','The only health effect the stimulus describes is improvement for the many people who limit their intake. Could someone else''s health get worse? Maybe, but nothing in the statements says so, and a Must Be True answer needs proof, not possibility.'),
29	('9d203d1a-6832-4fce-bcb2-7c0b8cc90f70'::uuid,'5613dc5f733ad54c7522f8a60fa73921','↓TC → ↑C runs the chain backward. Lower congestion sits at the far right: it''s what higher profits require. A requirement doesn''t trigger anything. Congestion could fall while the cost of living and the number of residents stay exactly where they are. The valid version goes the other way: ↑C → ↓TC.'),
30	('e338d583-4982-45f7-9c6c-b5716cdd2329'::uuid,'b8fdb2ac3bfd5fe54cd36d708648de56','Start at the left end. A lower cost of living guarantees more consumers living downtown (second statement), and more consumers guarantees higher profits (first statement). Two links, so ↓CL → ↑P.
31	
32	The move on a chain question: find the term that is the result of one rule and the trigger of another, connect them, then check each answer by asking whether its "if" sits to the left of its "then" on your chain.'),
33	('341e2b59-68f5-4027-83a0-0018d9606aa2'::uuid,'49467b64dbeb8579e18037c1872ff766','C starts from the right end of the chain, which triggers nothing, and lands on an increase in the cost of living, which no rule even mentions. The statements only cover what follows a decrease in the cost of living. Nothing could prove the cost goes up.'),
34	('7dbb893a-33e7-4a2b-898b-627e3bb7fc00'::uuid,'0ce122e75f4751ffc12da90ccc9f8a2e','D is the full chain read in reverse. The statements give ↓CL → ↓TC: if the cost of living falls, congestion must fall too. D flips it to ↓TC → ↓CL. Lower congestion is only a requirement for higher profits, so it can''t send us back up the chain.
35	
36	This is the most tempting trap because the two terms really are linked. Only the direction is wrong.'),
37	('972db7df-6686-420e-b5a9-11dd101ad4c9'::uuid,'da66f04d00d736c89ffeaf8aa0cddb15','The first statement says more consumers → higher profits. E reverses it: higher profits → more consumers. Profits could rise for some other reason, like more shoppers commuting in, and the statements never say residents are the only way to raise profits.'),
38	('f017809c-eba1-4690-b9ee-e7604fa70181'::uuid,'2975704debba45378b89107646d912cf','D substitutes one term for its partner. Claim 2 pairs each speed doubling with a cost doubling. Claim 1 says speed doubled because transistors doubled, so each transistor doubling is a speed doubling. Put transistors where speed was, and you get D. "Fabricating" is just another word for producing, and D keeps the mid-1990s window.
39	
40	When two statements share a term, try substituting one into the other. On many Must Be True questions, that substitution is the whole inference.'),
41	('2d2fe406-e5ce-4583-840d-a52161e420b4'::uuid,'51505aa016acb0a55db60ab5a1acefda','A reverses the rule. Extreme difficulty is required for addictiveness, not enough for it. A also shrinks "most users" to a single person. One person struggling to quit can''t satisfy a requirement about most users, and even satisfying it wouldn''t prove the substance is addictive.'),
42	('90fbac33-61e9-4516-997e-67dbee871ef4'::uuid,'e91eaeea96115ff93dc2e169ce2a825a','The expert compares an adequate definition with a rejected proposal, not with present practice. We have no count of what is deemed addictive now, so we can''t prove the number would shrink.'),
43	('c4dc1647-96ad-4328-9d6a-b8b4a0bdbb98'::uuid,'a715deae110602931a42149f98c1d45c','Let''s unpack C. Its subject is a substance some users can quit easily. It says that substance is addictive only if most users can''t quit easily:
44	
45	Addictive → NOT (most users quit with little or no difficulty)
46	
47	The expert''s rule gives Addictive → most users have extreme difficulty. If most users have extreme difficulty, it can''t be true that most quit with little or no difficulty. So C follows.
48	
49	The "some users" opening is what makes C look hard, but it''s only setup. A few easy quitters don''t decide anything, because the rule cares about most. When an answer wraps a rule in extra conditions, strip it to its arrow and compare it with the stimulus''s arrow.'),
50	('97165d62-07e7-4c1c-8861-fd500ca40145'::uuid,'0460d227e6f214fb26d0239a89a5f560','D talks about one person who used a substance without difficulty. The rule is about withdrawal causing difficulty for most users. Easy use says nothing about quitting, and one person says nothing about most. To conclude nonaddictive, we''d need the requirement to fail for most users, and D never shows that.'),
51	('de07c050-44d2-4d44-bdb8-13e62d7a2a29'::uuid,'38f9a97b2f65103933ffc32aab6397b8','The expert says what any adequate set of criteria must embody, which treats adequate criteria as possible. Disagreement over one proposed test doesn''t show the term can''t be defined precisely. Nothing supports "impossible."'),
52	('c75aa3a7-3401-497d-b02b-b4c882f18cb5'::uuid,'cbd2ab91c3bc4373651b978c378c42aa','A never says the word comes from an older work. If the correction fixes an obvious typo in a quotation from a modern work, rule 3 lets the editor correct it without explanation. And even in an older work, a word that occurs only once isn''t frequent, so rule 2, the only rule that calls for supplying an explanation, never triggers.'),
53	('c33e1704-8443-498b-8e31-4a8f638c1816'::uuid,'6df871ffe63d69ff3a1a0362ada26679','Rule 3 is the only rule about modern works, and it covers obvious typographical errors, not archaic spellings. Rules 1 and 2 cover older works only. Nothing in the manual permits modernizing an archaic spelling in a modern work, with or without an explanation.'),
54	('91e7e837-4afa-4412-aaf0-3f25a6ee17a7'::uuid,'757018dba439b8a4ee06f12a417907f4','The style manual never says an editor should modernize anything. Rule 2 gives permission ("may") when archaic forms occur frequently. Interference with comprehension only tells us rule 1''s preserve requirement doesn''t apply. Escaping a duty to preserve isn''t the same as gaining a duty to modernize.'),
55	('4222be4e-c90c-4c88-9bae-76474b680a0b'::uuid,'84ba9297cb6e2f8596869152b0d0650c','D gives us punctuation quoted from an older work that occurs frequently. That''s the full trigger for rule 2, so the editor may modernize it. The extra detail, that it interferes with comprehension, doesn''t hurt: a rule still applies when you know more than its trigger. And D keeps the manual''s "may" instead of upgrading it to "should."
56	
57	On rule-application questions, check two things: is the whole trigger present, and does the answer keep the rule''s strength?'),
58	('226569f5-8de0-449f-9c0c-3084624242ac'::uuid,'352f366262eccb6d1511d0b17b8c61b4','Rule 2 allows a general statement in the preface when similar modernizing has been done in more than one quotation. E describes modernizing only one instance, so the preface option isn''t triggered. E also turns the manual''s options into a "should": the manual says where an explanation can go, not that it must go in the preface.')
59	) v(id,ob,nb) where t.id=v.id and md5(t.body)=v.ob returning t.id;

Profits could rise for some other reason, like more shoppers commuting in, and the statements never say residents are the only way to raise profits.'),\n('f017809c-eba1-4690-b9ee-e7604fa70181'::uuid,'2975704debba45378b89107646d912cf','D substitutes one term for its partner. Claim 2 pairs each speed doubling with a cost doubling. Claim 1 says speed doubled because transistors doubled, so each transistor doubling is a speed doubling. Put transistors where speed was, and you get D. \"Fabricating\" is just another word for producing, and D keeps the mid-1990s window.\n\nWhen two statements share a term, try substituting one into the other. On many Must Be True questions, that substitution is the whole inference.'),\n('2d2fe406-e5ce-4583-840d-a52161e420b4'::uuid,'51505aa016acb0a55db60ab5a1acefda','A reverses the rule. Extreme difficulty is required for addictiveness, not enough for it. A also shrinks \"most users\" to a single person. One person struggling to quit can''t satisfy a requirement about most users, and even satisfying it wouldn''t prove the substance is addictive.'),\n('90fbac33-61e9-4516-997e-67dbee871ef4'::uuid,'e91eaeea96115ff93dc2e169ce2a825a','The expert compares an adequate definition with a rejected proposal, not with present practice. We have no count of what is deemed addictive now, so we can''t prove the number would shrink.'),\n('c4dc1647-96ad-4328-9d6a-b8b4a0bdbb98'::uuid,'a715deae110602931a42149f98c1d45c','Let''s unpack C. Its subject is a substance some users can quit easily. It says that substance is addictive only if most users can''t quit easily:\n\nAddictive → NOT (most users quit with little or no difficulty)\n\nThe expert''s rule gives Addictive → most users have extreme difficulty. If most users have extreme difficulty, it can''t be true that most quit with little or no difficulty. So C follows.\n\nThe \"some users\" opening is what makes C look hard, but it''s only setup. A few easy quitters don''t decide anything, because the rule cares about most. When an answer wraps a rule in extra conditions, strip it to its arrow and compare it with the stimulus''s arrow.'),\n('97165d62-07e7-4c1c-8861-fd500ca40145'::uuid,'0460d227e6f214fb26d0239a89a5f560','D talks about one person who used a substance without difficulty. The rule is about withdrawal causing difficulty for most users. Easy use says nothing about quitting, and one person says nothing about most. To conclude nonaddictive, we''d need the requirement to fail for most users, and D never shows that.'),\n('de07c050-44d2-4d44-bdb8-13e62d7a2a29'::uuid,'38f9a97b2f65103933ffc32aab6397b8','The expert says what any adequate set of criteria must embody, which treats adequate criteria as possible. Disagreement over one proposed test doesn''t show the term can''t be defined precisely. Nothing supports \"impossible.\"'),\n('c75aa3a7-3401-497d-b02b-b4c882f18cb5'::uuid,'cbd2ab91c3bc4373651b978c378c42aa','A never says the word comes from an older work. If the correction fixes an obvious typo in a quotation from a modern work, rule 3 lets the editor correct it without explanation. And even in an older work, a word that occurs only once isn''t frequent, so rule 2, the only rule that calls for supplying an explanation, never triggers.'),\n('c33e1704-8443-498b-8e31-4a8f638c1816'::uuid,'6df871ffe63d69ff3a1a0362ada26679','Rule 3 is the only rule about modern works, and it covers obvious typographical errors, not archaic spellings. Rules 1 and 2 cover older works only. Nothing in the manual permits modernizing an archaic spelling in a modern work, with or without an explanation.'),\n('91e7e837-4afa-4412-aaf0-3f25a6ee17a7'::uuid,'757018dba439b8a4ee06f12a417907f4','The style manual never says an editor should modernize anything. Rule 2 gives permission (\"may\") when archaic forms occur frequently. Interference with comprehension only tells us rule 1''s preserve requirement doesn''t apply. Escaping a duty to preserve isn''t the same as gaining a duty to modernize.'),\n('4222be4e-c90c-4c88-9bae-76474b680a0b'::uuid,'84ba9297cb6e2f8596869152b0d0650c','D gives us punctuation quoted from an older work that occurs frequently. That''s the full trigger for rule 2, so the editor may modernize it. The extra detail, that it interferes with comprehension, doesn''t hurt: a rule still applies when you know more than its trigger. And D keeps the manual''s \"may\" instead of upgrading it to \"should.\"\n\nOn rule-application questions, check two things: is the whole trigger present, and does the answer keep the rule''s strength?'),\n('226569f5-8de0-449f-9c0c-3084624242ac'::uuid,'352f366262eccb6d1511d0b17b8c61b4','Rule 2 allows a general statement in the preface when similar modernizing has been done in more than one quotation. E describes modernizing only one instance, so the preface option isn''t triggered. E also turns the manual''s options into a \"should\": the manual says where an explanation can go, not that it must go in the preface.')\n) v(id,ob,nb) where t.id=v.id and md5(t.body)=v.ob returning t.id;"}

{"project_id": "53b9a6f2-aba7-4ae4-8dd1-fa5b8aab4d76", "sql": "insert into lr_explanation_steps (explanation_id,position,label,body) select v.e,v.p,v.l,v.b from (values\n('3937fc73-7987-4439-80cc-6b64375df558'::uuid,1,'Goal','Since nothing forces any one author in or out, expect a conditional answer: K → ~L or its contrapositive, L → ~K.\n\nAny answer that makes a flat claim about one author, or about how many authors appear, can be tested the same way: build a legal book that breaks it. If you can, it doesn''t have to be true.'),\n('1df1c56c-2734-48a2-9856-6a70bf7258cb'::uuid,1,'Evaluate','Three conditionals. Is there a term they share?\n\nWillingness to compromise shows up twice. Mediation requires it (first rule), and ideological conflicts lack it (third rule). That overlap is the hinge. Flip the first rule with its contrapositive and attach it to the third:\n\nI → ~WC\n~WC → ~M\n\nSo: I → ~WC → ~M.\n\nWhat about litigation? L → SC shares no term with the other two. Being sure of your position never connects to compromise or ideology, so that rule is a dead end. Any answer that bridges it to the others is inventing a link.'),\n('1df1c56c-2734-48a2-9856-6a70bf7258cb'::uuid,2,'Goal','Predict I → ~M: people in ideological conflicts should not undergo mediation.\n\nThen watch for two traps: answers that start from a negated trigger or a necessary condition (those trigger nothing), and answers that try to connect the litigation rule to anything else.'),\n('73c0e56c-6943-42cd-ac7c-f2720d27b25d'::uuid,1,'Evaluate','Look for the shared term. \"Easier to limit, but not eliminate\" is the result of the second sentence and the trigger of the third. That lets us chain them:\n\nListed → Easier to limit → Many people limit → Their health improves\n\nNow the first sentence. It''s a fact, and it negates the start of the chain: caffeine content is not listed. A negated trigger tells us nothing, so the chain only describes what would happen if the content were listed. Any answer about what happens because it isn''t listed is going past the statements.'),\n('73c0e56c-6943-42cd-ac7c-f2720d27b25d'::uuid,2,'Goal','Predict the chain from start to finish, kept hypothetical: if exact caffeine content were listed, some people''s health would improve.\n\nWatch for answers that run the chain from \"not listed,\" and answers that swap limiting for eliminating.'),\n('fa9d395e-6f34-483b-8af6-e2d7a964a3f2'::uuid,1,'Evaluate','Three conditionals, and they overlap. More consumers is the result of the second and the trigger of the first. Higher profits is the result of the first and the trigger of the third (\"not increase unless\" puts lower congestion on the necessary side). Line them up:\n\n↓CL → ↑C → ↑P → ↓TC\n\nRead the chain like a one-way street. Anything on the left guarantees everything to its right. Nothing on the right guarantees anything to its left. Lower congestion is required for higher profits, but it doesn''t produce them.\n\nThe contrapositive runs the other way with every term negated: if congestion doesn''t fall, profits won''t rise, the number of residents won''t increase, and the cost of living won''t decrease.'),\n('fa9d395e-6f34-483b-8af6-e2d7a964a3f2'::uuid,2,'Goal','Every answer is a conditional, so the test is direction. A correct answer moves left to right along the chain, or right to left with both sides negated. Expect something like ↓CL → ↑P, ↑C → ↓TC, or ↓CL → ↓TC.\n\nAny answer that starts at ↓TC and claims something follows is backwards.'),\n('fa360b2e-cdb0-4824-80b2-17740d6bbb08'::uuid,1,'Evaluate','What do the two claims share? Doubling in computing speed. Claim 1 ties each transistor doubling to a speed doubling. Claim 2 ties each speed doubling, in that window, to a cost doubling. Connect them through the shared term:\n\nTransistors double → speed doubles → (mid-1990s into next decade) cost doubles\n\nNow notice the limits. The cost fact covers only the mid-1990s into the next decade. Nothing tells us why costs doubled, what happened to the retail price of computers, what engineers were trying to do, or whether the pattern will continue.'),\n('fa360b2e-cdb0-4824-80b2-17740d6bbb08'::uuid,2,'Goal','Predict the substitution, with its time window intact: from the mid-1990s into the next decade, each doubling in transistors came with a doubling in production cost.\n\nExpect wrong answers to stretch past what was reported: the only way to raise speed, retail prices, engineers'' motives, or the future.'),\n('92c75e79-e4b4-40b3-a28b-6e2b1286aeb1'::uuid,1,'Evaluate','The only conditional is the last sentence. Addictive substances have to be hard to quit for most users. Contrapositive: if withdrawal does not cause most users extreme difficulty, the substance is not addictive.\n\nNow ask what the rejected test missed. A few users quitting tells us about some users. The requirement is about most users. Both can be true at once: a substance can be easy to quit for a handful and brutal for the majority. That''s exactly how the prime examples of addictive substances slip past the some-users test.\n\nNotice also what the rule can''t do. It gives a requirement for addictiveness. It never says what is enough to make something addictive.'),\n('92c75e79-e4b4-40b3-a28b-6e2b1286aeb1'::uuid,2,'Goal','Expect an answer that applies the requirement in the right direction, probably playing some against most: a substance some users quit easily can still be addictive, but only if most users have a hard time.\n\nBe ready to reject answers that treat the requirement as sufficient, or that talk about one person instead of most users.'),\n('6f0a8af5-c592-4ba7-b022-e821e909ea5d'::uuid,1,'Evaluate','Watch the modal words. Rule 1 says \"are to be preserved\": a requirement. Rule 2 says \"may\": permission, not a duty. Rule 3 also says \"may.\" An answer that turns a \"may\" into a \"should\" goes beyond the manual.\n\nThen watch the triggers. Rule 2 needs only one thing: archaic material from an older work that occurs frequently. Whether it interferes doesn''t matter. Rule 3 covers obvious typos in modern works, not archaic spellings. And the manual is silent about some cases, like an archaic form that occurs infrequently but does interfere. Neither rule 1 nor rule 2 triggers there, so nothing follows.'),\n('6f0a8af5-c592-4ba7-b022-e821e909ea5d'::uuid,2,'Goal','Look for an answer that triggers a rule cleanly and keeps its strength. The likeliest shape: archaic spelling or punctuation from an older work that occurs frequently may be modernized. Extra details are fine as long as the whole trigger is there.')\n) v(e,p,l,b) where not exists (select 1 from lr_explanation_steps x where x.explanation_id=v.e and x.position=v.p) returning id;"}

17

22	  - The public actions, or inactions, of celebrities and of people who are widely respected are widely emulated.
23	  - Some celebrities do not vote.
24	  - Serious harm befalls a society in which many people refrain from voting.','Given','Given'),
25	('d46ae81c-0089-4b1b-a04c-f4f4110fc495'::uuid,'55b9bc7236552fa3bb49cc5e58a55630','Look for ideas that show up in more than one statement and chain them.
26	
27	Public inactions of widely respected people are widely emulated. Not voting is an inaction. So if a widely respected person publicly refrains from voting, many people may refrain too. Many people refraining brings serious harm. That gives us a chain:
28	widely respected person publicly doesn''t vote → many people don''t vote → serious harm to society
29	
30	Now the first statement applies. Publicly not voting has the potential to produce serious harm, so one should not do it.
31	
32	Notice what the chain does not need: the third statement. "Some celebrities do not vote" doesn''t say they do it publicly, so it doesn''t fire anything. It''s there to tempt you into an answer about celebrities who don''t vote.','Evaluate','Evaluate'),
33	('7c4b65b6-6626-4bf5-abff-c35b8341a81b'::uuid,'5aa2d57e51b78471b701639f9328937e','Look for a "should not" principle about people whose actions are emulated: widely respected people (or celebrities) should not publicly refrain from voting. Be wary of answers that tell society what to require, tell people whom to respect or emulate, or tell anyone they must vote. The stimulus only says what one should not do.','Goal','Goal'),
34	('6909eea9-13b1-407d-acb8-597c73c737a2'::uuid,'7fcbb73330f980b9804d42d596775020','1. No new course will be approved unless the committee or Dean Wilson has already received a proposal for it.
35	new course approved → proposal received by committee or by Dean Wilson
36	
37	2. Dean Wilson has received only one new course proposal.
38	
39	3. All new course proposals the committee has received are for upper-level courses.
40	committee proposal → upper-level
41	
42	4. Beginning next year, all upper-level courses will have prerequisites.
43	upper-level → prerequisite','Given','Given'),
44	('e5034862-ccee-462e-a917-35aeaee2425b'::uuid,'419ee3cbbc71701b7ae919f9d518210b','Statements 3 and 4 chain together:
45	committee proposal → upper-level → prerequisite
46	
47	Now combine that with statement 1. Every new course next year came from one of two places. If it came from the committee, it has a prerequisite. If it came from Dean Wilson, we know nothing about it, but statement 2 says the dean has only one proposal.
48	
49	So the dean''s pile can supply at most one new course. Every other new course must come from the committee, and so must have a prerequisite. Put plainly: at most one new course next year can lack a prerequisite.
50	
51	Also notice what''s missing. Receiving a proposal is required for approval, but nothing says any proposal will be approved. And the prerequisite rule covers upper-level courses only, not every course.','Evaluate','Evaluate'),
52	('0d45798d-2be6-440a-9948-b9e95fcd763f'::uuid,'d2f36bdcd4e947363f471b1562dfe931','"Moral excellence can be achieved only by repeatedly overcoming inclinations to do the wrong thing."
53	moral excellence → repeatedly overcame inclinations to do wrong
54	
55	Overcoming these inclinations is often difficult, even for a morally virtuous person.
56	
57	"the only way to become a morally virtuous person is through the achievement of moral excellence."
58	morally virtuous → moral excellence','Given','Given'),
59	('0646e18d-1d86-4c60-ae80-2d65c5eeb4ef'::uuid,'46fbf1703ec3adc5ff8aa7d39450ebfb','Two requirement rules share a term: moral excellence. It''s the result of the virtue rule and the trigger of the excellence rule, so they chain:
60	morally virtuous → moral excellence → repeatedly overcame inclinations to do wrong
61	
62	So every morally virtuous person has repeatedly overcome inclinations to do the wrong thing. Now take one more small step. You can''t overcome an inclination you never had. So every morally virtuous person has had inclinations to do wrong.
63	
64	The arrows only run one way. Moral excellence is required for virtue, not enough for it. Overcoming inclinations is required for excellence, not enough for it.','Evaluate','Evaluate'),
65	('8c07262c-c721-42c3-81b4-9d63b4592b86'::uuid,'d85f7e04da740717b27a19e60bd6d774','Expect the end of the chain, said about virtuous people: every morally virtuous person has repeatedly overcome, and so has had, inclinations to do wrong. Watch for answers that run an arrow backward or negate both sides.','Goal','Goal'),
66	('8ff6050d-272c-4107-b9f4-b1ad274ce116'::uuid,'a61efa8edac5459be071ce3cacf84857','The report sets up a problem and then a fix. The problem: in a set a few inches thick, a noncompound screen gets dimmer as it gets larger, so thin, large and bright don''t go together. The fix: compound screens are made of small, bright tiles, and you can add as many tiles as you want without losing brightness or adding thickness.
67	
68	Put those together. Keep adding tiles and the screen gets as large as you like, stays bright, and the set stays a few inches thick. So thin sets with screens that are both bright and very large are now possible.','Evaluate','Evaluate'),
69	('994af839-0cfb-4afe-a4f6-d898ea77c2e1'::uuid,'eaa1cd8ac1d19c4bf4b91abd3a5f8700','Rule (if):
70	based on info from a reliable source → reasonable to maintain
71	
72	Fact (some): some beliefs are
73	1. based on info from a reliable source, and
74	2. not self-evident, and
75	3. not grounded in observable evidence','Statements','Statements'),
76	('7ffd282a-12bf-4803-81b1-20487a2d66ae'::uuid,'06779a368c97fa69a334d3782d4e40b7','We have one conditional and one fact. With a conditional on Must Be True, ask two questions:
77	1. Is there another conditional to chain it with?
78	2. Does any fact trigger it (or its contrapositive)?
79	
80	There''s no second conditional, so #1 is out. For #2, the "some" beliefs in the second sentence are based on information from a reliable source. That triggers the rule, so those beliefs are reasonable to maintain.
81	
82	Now that group has four traits at once: reliable source, reasonable, not self-evident, and not grounded in observable evidence. The question is most likely testing whether we can attach "reasonable" to the other traits in that group.
83	
84	Two limits to keep in mind. A "some" fact is about one group, so it can''t become a rule about all beliefs. And the rule only says a reliable source is enough for reasonableness, not that it''s the only route.','Evaluate','Evaluate'),

The financial predicament \"would not have been resolved if the traffic flow across the bridge during rush hour had not been increased.\"\nno increase in rush-hour flow → predicament not resolved\npredicament resolved → increase in rush-hour flow (contrapositive)','Explanation','Statements'),\n('5412f9a3-8035-4b00-b2bf-04a8aa800dbf'::uuid,'73a94846e5b91c6f0b06e32df4b8eb6d','Coastal estuaries are easily polluted by nutrient-rich sewage.\n\nWhen that pollution overnutrifies the water, algae proliferate.\nsewage overnutrifies water → algae proliferate\n\nThe abundant algae \"sometimes\" feed microorganisms that are toxic to fish, killing most of the fish.\nabundant algae → (sometimes) toxic microorganisms thrive → most fish die','Given','Given'),\n('07a04192-5610-42df-931d-1efaaee6898d'::uuid,'37301ab4471d0431449e9cc80739fbc5','Some nurseries label any Stark Sweet Melody nectarine trees \"miniature.\" Others do not.\n\nRule: if a variety of fruit tree is not suitable for growing in a tub or a pot, no tree of that variety can be correctly labeled miniature.\nvariety not suitable for tub or pot → no tree of it is correctly labeled \"miniature\"\ncorrectly labeled \"miniature\" → variety suitable for tub or pot (contrapositive)','Explanation','Statements'),\n('50a4f069-39d5-4963-bca5-2e241e4ba078'::uuid,'a3300b0adc4111bf7655e60818df56ea','  - One should not do anything that has the potential to produce serious harm to one''s society.\n  - The public actions, or inactions, of celebrities and of people who are widely respected are widely emulated.\n  - Some celebrities do not vote.\n  - Serious harm befalls a society in which many people refrain from voting.','Given','Given'),\n('d46ae81c-0089-4b1b-a04c-f4f4110fc495'::uuid,'55b9bc7236552fa3bb49cc5e58a55630','Look for ideas that show up in more than one statement and chain them.\n\nPublic inactions of widely respected people are widely emulated. Not voting is an inaction. So if a widely respected person publicly refrains from voting, many people may refrain too. Many people refraining brings serious harm. That gives us a chain:\nwidely respected person publicly doesn''t vote → many people don''t vote → serious harm to society\n\nNow the first statement applies. Publicly not voting has the potential to produce serious harm, so one should not do it.\n\nNotice what the chain does not need: the third statement. \"Some celebrities do not vote\" doesn''t say they do it publicly, so it doesn''t fire anything. It''s there to tempt you into an answer about celebrities who don''t vote.','Evaluate','Evaluate'),\n('7c4b65b6-6626-4bf5-abff-c35b8341a81b'::uuid,'5aa2d57e51b78471b701639f9328937e','Look for a \"should not\" principle about people whose actions are emulated: widely respected people (or celebrities) should not publicly refrain from voting. Be wary of answers that tell society what to require, tell people whom to respect or emulate, or tell anyone they must vote. The stimulus only says what one should not do.','Goal','Goal'),\n('6909eea9-13b1-407d-acb8-597c73c737a2'::uuid,'7fcbb73330f980b9804d42d596775020','1. No new course will be approved unless the committee or Dean Wilson has already received a proposal for it.\nnew course approved → proposal received by committee or by Dean Wilson\n\n2. Dean Wilson has received only one new course proposal.\n\n3. All new course proposals the committee has received are for upper-level courses.\ncommittee proposal → upper-level\n\n4. Beginning next year, all upper-level courses will have prerequisites.\nupper-level → prerequisite','Given','Given'),\n('e5034862-ccee-462e-a917-35aeaee2425b'::uuid,'419ee3cbbc71701b7ae919f9d518210b','Statements 3 and 4 chain together:\ncommittee proposal → upper-level → prerequisite\n\nNow combine that with statement 1. Every new course next year came from one of two places. If it came from the committee, it has a prerequisite. If it came from Dean Wilson, we know nothing about it, but statement 2 says the dean has only one proposal.\n\nSo the dean''s pile can supply at most one new course. Every other new course must come from the committee, and so must have a prerequisite. Put plainly: at most one new course next year can lack a prerequisite.\n\nAlso notice what''s missing. Receiving a proposal is required for approval, but nothing says any proposal will be approved. And the prerequisite rule covers upper-level courses only, not every course.','Evaluate','Evaluate'),\n('0d45798d-2be6-440a-9948-b9e95fcd763f'::uuid,'d2f36bdcd4e947363f471b1562dfe931','\"Moral excellence can be achieved only by repeatedly overcoming inclinations to do the wrong thing.\"\nmoral excellence → repeatedly overcame inclinations to do wrong\n\nOvercoming these inclinations is often difficult, even for a morally virtuous person.\n\n\"the only way to become a morally virtuous person is through the achievement of moral excellence.\"\nmorally virtuous → moral excellence','Given','Given'),\n('0646e18d-1d86-4c60-ae80-2d65c5eeb4ef'::uuid,'46fbf1703ec3adc5ff8aa7d39450ebfb','Two requirement rules share a term: moral excellence. It''s the result of the virtue rule and the trigger of the excellence rule, so they chain:\nmorally virtuous → moral excellence → repeatedly overcame inclinations to do wrong\n\nSo every morally virtuous person has repeatedly overcome inclinations to do the wrong thing. Now take one more small step. You can''t overcome an inclination you never had. So every morally virtuous person has had inclinations to do wrong.\n\nThe arrows only run one way. Moral excellence is required for virtue, not enough for it. Overcoming inclinations is required for excellence, not enough for it.','Evaluate','Evaluate'),\n('8c07262c-c721-42c3-81b4-9d63b4592b86'::uuid,'d85f7e04da740717b27a19e60bd6d774','Expect the end of the chain, said about virtuous people: every morally virtuous person has repeatedly overcome, and so has had, inclinations to do wrong. Watch for answers that run an arrow backward or negate both sides.','Goal','Goal'),\n('8ff6050d-272c-4107-b9f4-b1ad274ce116'::uuid,'a61efa8edac5459be071ce3cacf84857','The report sets up a problem and then a fix. The problem: in a set a few inches thick, a noncompound screen gets dimmer as it gets larger, so thin, large and bright don''t go together. The fix: compound screens are made of small, bright tiles, and you can add as many tiles as you want without losing brightness or adding thickness.\n\nPut those together. Keep adding tiles and the screen gets as large as you like, stays bright, and the set stays a few inches thick. So thin sets with screens that are both bright and very large are now possible.','Evaluate','Evaluate'),\n('994af839-0cfb-4afe-a4f6-d898ea77c2e1'::uuid,'eaa1cd8ac1d19c4bf4b91abd3a5f8700','Rule (if):\nbased on info from a reliable source → reasonable to maintain\n\nFact (some): some beliefs are\n1. based on info from a reliable source, and\n2. not self-evident, and\n3. not grounded in observable evidence','Statements','Statements'),\n('7ffd282a-12bf-4803-81b1-20487a2d66ae'::uuid,'06779a368c97fa69a334d3782d4e40b7','We have one conditional and one fact. With a conditional on Must Be True, ask two questions:\n1. Is there another conditional to chain it with?\n2. Does any fact trigger it (or its contrapositive)?\n\nThere''s no second conditional, so #1 is out. For #2, the \"some\" beliefs in the second sentence are based on information from a reliable source. That triggers the rule, so those beliefs are reasonable to maintain.\n\nNow that group has four traits at once: reliable source, reasonable, not self-evident, and not grounded in observable evidence. The question is most likely testing whether we can attach \"reasonable\" to the other traits in that group.\n\nTwo limits to keep in mind. A \"some\" fact is about one group, so it can''t become a rule about all beliefs. And the rule only says a reliable source is enough for reasonableness, not that it''s the only route.','Evaluate','Evaluate'),\n('99fa7637-eddf-47b6-bba2-a652c22a630f'::uuid,'15cd0176cdd4d465c919e6e9601f5efe','Look for a \"some\" statement that pairs reasonable with one or both of the other traits: some reasonable beliefs are not self-evident, some reasonable beliefs are not grounded in observable evidence, or some reasonable beliefs are neither.','Goal','Goal')\n) v(id,ob,nb,ol,nl) where t.id=v.id and md5(t.body)=v.ob returning t.id;"}

2	('cbdecbe8-ae3b-4bf8-8309-586d3c924c8c'::uuid,1,'Evaluate','Both sentences are conditionals, and they share one idea: the increase in rush-hour traffic flow. When two rules share a term, try to chain them.
3	
4	The increase is the result in the first rule and the trigger in the second:
5	no investment → no increase in rush-hour flow → predicament not resolved
6	
7	Read it forward: without the computer modeling investment, there''s no increase, and without the increase, the predicament stays unresolved. Or read the contrapositive: resolving the predicament required the increase, and the increase required the investment.
8	
9	Each link is a requirement. The investment was needed; nothing says it was enough. So the safe inferences are about what could not have happened without something, not about what was guaranteed to happen.'),
10	('cbdecbe8-ae3b-4bf8-8309-586d3c924c8c'::uuid,2,'Goal','Look for the two ends of the chain joined together. Something like: if the city had not invested in computer modeling technology, the financial predicament would not have been resolved. The contrapositive version (resolving the predicament required the investment) would work just as well.'),
11	('ac2194b1-6d03-4995-b8f9-556aa1f12fa4'::uuid,1,'Evaluate','Each sentence picks up where the last one ended: sewage leads to overnutrified water, overnutrified water leads to algae, and algae can lead to a fish kill. When causes and effects line up end to end like this, connect the first cause to the last effect.
12	
13	Watch the word "sometimes" on the last link. The algae don''t always feed toxic microorganisms. So the chain doesn''t prove that sewage always kills the fish. It proves that it can.'),
14	('ac2194b1-6d03-4995-b8f9-556aa1f12fa4'::uuid,2,'Goal','Look for a softly worded answer that joins the start of the chain to the end: overnutrifying an estuary with sewage can lead to most of its fish dying. An answer that says this "will" happen goes past the "sometimes".'),
15	('ef68a7e2-3ce5-47c5-9918-a96762181a53'::uuid,1,'Evaluate','We have one rule and one fact. The rule works on a variety''s suitability. The fact is about one variety: some nurseries call every Stark Sweet Melody tree "miniature."
16	
17	Can we fire the rule? Only if we know whether Stark Sweet Melody is suitable for a tub or pot, and we''re never told. So we can''t say anyone is mislabeling outright.
18	
19	What we can do is put the inference in conditional form. Suppose Stark Sweet Melody is not suitable. Then none of its trees can be correctly labeled "miniature." But some nurseries label them "miniature." So those nurseries are mislabeling.
20	
21	Also notice what the rule doesn''t give us. Suitability is required for a correct "miniature" label, but it isn''t enough. Even a suitable variety might not be miniature.'),
22	('ef68a7e2-3ce5-47c5-9918-a96762181a53'::uuid,2,'Goal','Look for an answer that keeps the unknown as a condition: "If Stark Sweet Melody is not suitable for a tub or pot, then some nurseries are mislabeling it." It might be phrased with "unless," which means "if not."'),
23	('4e360875-0755-4a5a-850a-ef5d076a133c'::uuid,2,'Goal','Look for an answer built on the "at most one exception" idea: if there are two or more new courses, at least one has a prerequisite. Another safe version: any new course that didn''t come from Dean Wilson''s proposal has a prerequisite. Reject answers that assume a proposal gets approved, or that stretch the prerequisite rule past upper-level courses.'),
24	('92043ea4-ffbd-42ba-b249-6faaf3768e45'::uuid,2,'Goal','Look for the fix stated as a capability: thin television sets can now have screens that are both large and bright. The "However" and "Moreover" tell us the report is building toward exactly that. Reject answers about what people want, what''s wrong with the new screens, or how thickness changes brightness.')

D says not virtuous → no excellence, which negates both sides without flipping them. The valid contrapositive is no excellence → not virtuous.
