41	('9f4ef585-edda-41b5-b5ea-61fc558935a1'::uuid,'0f3dd48fd9ff9df6759c1a9bc53b6891','Chain the two rules: virtue requires excellence, and excellence requires repeatedly overcoming inclinations to do wrong. So every virtuous person has overcome such inclinations, and you can''t overcome an inclination you never had.
42	
43	The move to repeat: when two "only" rules share a term, connect the outer ends, then ask what the final requirement itself presupposes. The right answer here states that presupposition.'),
44	('9bf9af78-c1ff-4171-8855-60df2e39885f'::uuid,'ed5cae321750368076a01c683c2fe1b3','Nothing in the report counts against small screens. It says unlimited tiles can be joined, not that a screen needs many tiles. A compound screen of just a few bright tiles fits everything we''re told.'),
45	('39a9401b-5cd4-4c88-ae7f-5858da4e7447'::uuid,'101abb4c5ddd848e4dae857a69bbc618','The report is about what the technology can do, not what buyers want. Test it: every sentence could be true even if nobody wanted to buy one of these sets. Demand is a new topic.'),
46	('3094c624-6649-4953-a36b-6587ea8759fb'::uuid,'ed4cd6ea44cc9148d4f1d8b64b815933','The report describes size and brightness at one fixed thickness: "a set of this thickness." It never changes the thickness, so it can''t tell us what a thicker set does to brightness. C invents a second relationship from a sentence that held thickness constant.'),
47	('15f1e9c6-1913-4426-b843-71cb92a57ccb'::uuid,'b62d7d0ffd3a59c1b4227ec5dfccf863','This is the problem and the fix put together. Noncompound screens in thin sets get dimmer as they grow. Compound screens are thin, each tile is bright, and unlimited tiles can be added without losing brightness or adding thickness. So a thin set can now have a screen that''s both bright and very large.
48	
49	The move to repeat: when a stimulus states a limitation and then says "however" and "moreover" about a new approach, the inference is usually that the new approach gets past that limitation.'),
50	('9071ab01-af53-4183-b3f6-ba3609cf6036'::uuid,'282ddd0fd083ad0f64e02b3497ee225f','The report lists advantages. It never says those are the only differences. Cost, resolution or durability could all be worse with compound screens, and nothing in the report rules that out. Silence about disadvantages doesn''t prove there are none.'),
51	('79776865-8d4b-4b95-bf94-665de1d5b8b4'::uuid,'2ec27b383d884592baecf2ab71d4a06f','The stimulus proves the opposite for some beliefs. The beliefs in the second sentence aren''t grounded in observable evidence, yet they come from a reliable source and so are reasonable. A belief can lack observable evidence and still be reasonable.'),
52	('5ac3e540-b9bb-4d34-920e-33fcea124682'::uuid,'94dd89528a9246a806f4bf0eab0adc71','The second sentence directly contradicts this. It describes beliefs that are based on a reliable source and are not self-evident. One counterexample is enough to sink an "all" claim, and the stimulus hands us that counterexample.'),
53	('6b221977-e312-4303-8fab-e3861fa7b159'::uuid,'b462f419ece11dd33b3e57b17905b5f1','The rule runs reliable source → reasonable. C runs it backward: reasonable (with no observable evidence) → reliable source. A reliable source is one way to make a belief reasonable, not the only way. A reasonable belief could rest on something else entirely.'),
54	('df219328-2674-438e-9f17-2b4ff1f8a6af'::uuid,'1f8554d206c3295b5f70ef4b36b260ad','This turns a "some" fact into a rule. The second sentence shows some beliefs lack both traits, but a group that lacks both doesn''t prove that lacking one forces lacking the other. Nothing rules out a belief that is self-evident yet not grounded in observable evidence.'),
55	('21b9fc7c-c685-4555-9802-c12811a5ff77'::uuid,'eb758e50ed392baedea71c902b2f3b42','Run the beliefs from the second sentence through the rule. They''re based on a reliable source, so they''re reasonable. They''re also not self-evident and not grounded in observable evidence. So among reasonable beliefs that aren''t self-evident, some aren''t grounded in observable evidence.
56	
57	The move to repeat: when a "some" fact triggers a rule, the rule''s result attaches to that group, and you can pair it with any other trait the group has. The right answer is often a "some" statement built from those traits.')
58	) v(id,ob,nb) where t.id=v.id and md5(t.body)=v.ob returning t.id;

Buying a competing package is still investing in computer modeling technology, so the requirement would be met. And meeting a requirement doesn''t guarantee anything, so we can''t say the predicament would have stayed unresolved.'),\n('5880ae4a-e75e-4d9e-87a7-1b8d3b654680'::uuid,'a1bcd3c5abbaecac54e97f363ee2e07b','This is the chain with the middle link removed. So no investment means no resolution.\n\nThe move to repeat: when two conditionals share a term, line them up so the shared term is the result of one and the trigger of the other, then connect the outer ends. Check the direction too. B keeps the \"not\" on both sides in the same order the rules give them, so it follows.'),\n('857f0842-9bec-472d-a187-7738d81adba7'::uuid,'47632ed0a408edb695cafb503a0052f6','The stimulus only tells us about rush-hour flow. When a chain has a weak link, the right answer keeps that weakness in its wording.'),\n('82131486-4dbf-4f30-8846-a80cdceb4c08'::uuid,'3b1c74e33e6b46ae4e7286e0dae03638','\"Most nurseries\" is a claim about the whole industry. {"project_id": "53b9a6f2-aba7-4ae4-8dd1-fa5b8aab4d76", "sql": "insert into lr_explanation_steps (explanation_id,position,label,body) select v.e,v.p,v.l,v.b from (values\n('cbdecbe8-ae3b-4bf8-8309-586d3c924c8c'::uuid,1,'Evaluate','Both sentences are conditionals, and they share one idea: the increase in rush-hour traffic flow. When two rules share a term, try to chain them.\n\nThe increase is the result in the first rule and the trigger in the second:\nno investment → no increase in rush-hour flow → predicament not resolved\n\nRead it forward: without the computer modeling investment, there''s no increase, and without the increase, the predicament stays unresolved. Or read the contrapositive: resolving the predicament required the increase, and the increase required the investment.\n\nEach link is a requirement. The investment was needed; nothing says it was enough. So the safe inferences are about what could not have happened without something, not about what was guaranteed to happen.'),\n('cbdecbe8-ae3b-4bf8-8309-586d3c924c8c'::uuid,2,'Goal','Look for the two ends of the chain joined together. Something like: if the city had not invested in computer modeling technology, the financial predicament would not have been resolved. The contrapositive version (resolving the predicament required the investment) would work just as well.'),\n('ac2194b1-6d03-4995-b8f9-556aa1f12fa4'::uuid,1,'Evaluate','Each sentence picks up where the last one ended: sewage leads to overnutrified water, overnutrified water leads to algae, and algae can lead to a fish kill. When causes and effects line up end to end like this, connect the first cause to the last effect.\n\nWatch the word \"sometimes\" on the last link. The algae don''t always feed toxic microorganisms. So the chain doesn''t prove that sewage always kills the fish. It proves that it can.'),\n('ac2194b1-6d03-4995-b8f9-556aa1f12fa4'::uuid,2,'Goal','Look for a softly worded answer that joins the start of the chain to the end: overnutrifying an estuary with sewage can lead to most of its fish dying. An answer that says this \"will\" happen goes past the \"sometimes\".'),\n('ef68a7e2-3ce5-47c5-9918-a96762181a53'::uuid,1,'Evaluate','We have one rule and one fact. The rule works on a variety''s suitability. The fact is about one variety: some nurseries call every Stark Sweet Melody tree \"miniature.\"\n\nCan we fire the rule? Only if we know whether Stark Sweet Melody is suitable for a tub or pot, and we''re never told. So we can''t say anyone is mislabeling outright.\n\nWhat we can do is put the inference in conditional form. Suppose Stark Sweet Melody is not suitable. Then none of its trees can be correctly labeled \"miniature.\" But some nurseries label them \"miniature.\" So those nurseries are mislabeling.\n\nAlso notice what the rule doesn''t give us. Suitability is required for a correct \"miniature\" label, but it isn''t enough. Even a suitable variety might not be miniature.'),\n('ef68a7e2-3ce5-47c5-9918-a96762181a53'::uuid,2,'Goal','Look for an answer that keeps the unknown as a condition: \"If Stark Sweet Melody is not suitable for a tub or pot, then some nurseries are mislabeling it.\" It might be phrased with \"unless,\" which means \"if not.\"'),\n('4e360875-0755-4a5a-850a-ef5d076a133c'::uuid,2,'Goal','Look for an answer built on the \"at most one exception\" idea: if there are two or more new courses, at least one has a prerequisite. Another safe version: any new course that didn''t come from Dean Wilson''s proposal has a prerequisite. Reject answers that assume a proposal gets approved, or that stretch the prerequisite rule past upper-level courses.'),\n('92043ea4-ffbd-42ba-b249-6faaf3768e45'::uuid,2,'Goal','Look for the fix stated as a capability: thin television sets can now have screens that are both large and bright. The \"However\" and \"Moreover\" tell us the report is building toward exactly that. Reject answers about what people want, what''s wrong with the new screens, or how thickness changes brightness.')\n) v(e,p,l,b) where not exists (select 1 from lr_explanation_steps x where x.explanation_id=v.e and x.position=v.p) returning id;"}

Here the bridge is "lemur." The only primates native to Madagascar are lemurs, and lemurs are lower primates. Put those together: every primate native to Madagascar is a lower primate.
10	
11	Now ask what that rules out. Lower primates and higher primates are two separate groups, so a lower primate is not a higher primate. That means no primate native to Madagascar is a higher primate. Not a diurnal one, not a nocturnal one, not any kind.
12	
13	The last sentence is the tempting one, because it looks like it chains with the lemur sentence. 18	('bc3a398f-5239-4954-85b8-150de15bb487'::uuid,'ff0c24f92cdbc2a82e8786f81369feb7','Match up the parts of the sociologists'' response. The sociologists object that a complex phenomenon cannot be caused by a simple phenomenon.
19	
20	That objection only lands if Y is a simple phenomenon. If voters'' economic decisions were themselves complex, the sociologists'' rule would not touch the theory. So the sociologists apparently assume that Y is simple.','Evaluate','Evaluate'),
21	('47832198-bd32-4ead-ae25-2ab4f3e8e78b'::uuid,'3cac3607eb855e85ea3599bb155829aa','Look for an answer saying the sociologists treat voters'' economically driven decisions as a simple phenomenon, or at least as something that isn''t automatically complex.

24	('9257949a-230b-4b41-a4c4-abd07679c010'::uuid,'c9a998b9e12adcb03ecffd9cb25966bb','The citizen predicts a chain: a major tax cut for upper-income citizens, then a correspondingly large increase in investment, then new jobs. 25

27	
28	So the citizen needs, at a minimum, that the tax-cut money can go toward investment. It''s a small requirement, but the whole plan rests on it.','Evaluate','Evaluate'),
29	('2ba7efc6-5622-4ad3-8663-b4ca174d2aea'::uuid,'ecb824d3b71df012431583a3964da8a9','Expect a defender: an answer that rules out the objection "the tax-cut money can''t end up as investment." 30	('f1ab5847-6ef7-4571-97c9-15d2dac5a986'::uuid,'9be7417684d2b25aab48dc45a98b0b74','The scientist argues by analogy. Selective breeding is a crude form of genetic engineering, and people have done it for millennia, so genetic engineering is not unethical.
31	
32	What has to be true about selective breeding for that to work? It has to be acceptable. If selective breeding were itself unethical, showing that genetic engineering resembles it would only put genetic engineering in bad company. The millennia of practice don''t settle that question either. A practice can be very old and still wrong.
33	
34	There''s a second gap: is choosing which animals breed really the same kind of thing as directly manipulating genetic codes? The scientist treats them as one category, and a critic could dispute that. But the first gap is the one the argument can''t do without. The scientist never says selective breeding is ethical.','Evaluate','Evaluate'),
35	('e81c2c4a-d249-4334-b88c-446aad548525'::uuid,'3eb152713dcbfce68a168c3bc9da2de0','The answer will most likely protect the base of the analogy: selective breeding itself is not unethical. It could also defend the comparison, saying breeding and genetic-code manipulation are relevantly alike. 36	('7b91f97d-2de9-4390-ab49-d7c537e4a795'::uuid,'089fe55cad76fef3e04cb2314b3b1417','The evidence gives a trade-off. Presoaking saves time. Skipping it gives plumper beans. The conclusion says that when quality matters more than speed, skip the soak.

39	
40	So the author has to assume that plumper beans make for a better dish.','Evaluate','Evaluate')

5	Watch for two traps: an answer that makes bonuses the only way to save, and an answer that explains why the plan would work if it already worked.'),
6	('a2c47cef-4985-40e5-9b84-e604a10211eb'::uuid,3,'Goal','Expect a link between the conclusion''s new idea, a reasoned approach, and the evidence''s idea, injuring others. Something like: people who take a reasoned approach are less likely to injure others. Negate it, and reasoned people need government''s protection just as much, so there''s no reason for government''s power to shrink.')
7	) v(e,p,l,b) where not exists (select 1 from lr_explanation_steps x where x.explanation_id=v.e and x.position=v.p) returning id;

7	('ea62f47c-ca93-4465-a834-b51fde78e899'::uuid,'a74d53ada6c69dfc6007263adcbc5cba','This is the belief the objection runs on. 10	('91303727-b979-40ca-97e8-03e3c45302de'::uuid,'75dd551d62e04ed1f735e69a88af93ba','The sociologists'' rule only rules one thing out: a simple cause can''t produce a complex result. 12	('d598225c-6950-457b-9118-8100a31a6498'::uuid,'cd809889ee9c0da2c82b1dd337fae737','This is the reverse of what they believe.
